Getting started with varm

Source: vignettes/getting-started.Rmd
getting-started.Rmd

varm estimates reduced-form and structural VARs, Bayesian VARs (Minnesota, sum-of-coefficients, hierarchical, stochastic volatility, shrinkage priors), time-varying-parameter VARs and local projections, with a compiled (RcppArmadillo) engine. This tour takes about ten minutes and follows the workflow of a typical applied project:

  1. data, 2. lag choice, 3. estimation, 4. stability, 5. impulse responses with bands, 6. variance decomposition, 7. historical decomposition, 8. forecasts,
  2. a Bayesian VAR in three lines, 10. a local projection in three lines,
  3. the tidy workflow: tibbles into ggplot2.

The API follows tidy-tools conventions. Variables are selected with tidyselect (vars = c(infl, rate), shocks = rate), results convert to tibbles with tidy(), glance() and augment(), and every result has an autoplot() method that returns an ordinary ggplot2 object you can extend with + labs(), + theme_varm() or any other layer.

Every object returned by irf(), fevd(), hd() and forecast() is built from the same currency, a set of reduced-form parameter draws (draws()), so the frequentist (bootstrap) and Bayesian code paths share one interface.

1. Data

yraw holds three quarterly US series from the Koop-Korobilis data set (1953Q1 to 2006Q3): inflation (infl), the unemployment rate (unemp) and a short-term interest rate (rate). We add a Date column. varm() drops non-numeric columns from the estimation but keeps a Date column as the time axis of the plots.

y <- yraw
y$date <- seq(as.Date("1953-01-01"), by = "quarter", length.out = nrow(y))
dim(yraw)
#> [1] 215   3
long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("infl", "unemp", "rate"), function(v) {
  data.frame(date = y$date, variable = v, value = y[[v]])
}))
ggplot(long, aes(date, value)) +
  geom_line(colour = varm_palette(1)) +
  facet_wrap(vars(variable), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_varm()

varm() accepts a data frame (preferred), a matrix or a ts. Use vars = to pick the endogenous variables with tidyselect, for example varm(y, p = 2, vars = c(infl, rate)) for a bivariate system. All three series are persistent levels; we keep them in levels, which is standard for a VAR used for dynamics and forecasting (see vignette("var-theory"), “Reduced-form VAR: theory, inference and use”, for when this is and is not appropriate).

2. Lag choice

var_select() evaluates AIC, Hannan-Quinn (HQ), Schwarz (SC) and the (log) final prediction error (FPE) for p=1,…,pmaxp=1,\dots,p_{\max} on a common sample.

sel <- var_select(yraw, pmax = 8)
sel$selection
#> AIC  HQ  SC FPE 
#>   6   2   2   6

AIC and FPE favour long lags, HQ and SC pick p=2p=2. We take two lags as a parsimonious baseline.

3. Estimation 

fit <- varm(y, p = 2)
fit
#> <varm> VAR(2) with 3 variables, 213 effective observations
#> logLik = -338.416; max |eigenvalue| = 0.946
#> 
#>             infl   unemp    rate
#> infl.l1   1.5378 -0.0095  0.5457
#> unemp.l1 -0.2809  1.3297 -0.6475
#> rate.l1  -0.0571 -0.0210  0.7766
#> infl.l2  -0.5418  0.0341 -0.4395
#> unemp.l2  0.2336 -0.4290  0.6730
#> rate.l2   0.0580  0.0457  0.1232
#> const     0.2872  0.3654  0.0052

The tibble summaries are the quickest way to read a fit: tidy() is the coefficient table (one row per equation and regressor), glance() the one-row model summary and augment() the data with fitted values and residuals.

co <- tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE)
co[co$response == "rate", ]
#> # A tibble: 7 × 8
#>   response term     estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
#>   <chr>    <chr>       <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 rate     infl.l1   0.546      0.149     3.66   3.16e- 4   0.252      0.839
#> 2 rate     unemp.l1 -0.647      0.155    -4.17   4.47e- 5  -0.954     -0.341
#> 3 rate     rate.l1   0.777      0.0738   10.5    5.19e-21   0.631      0.922
#> 4 rate     infl.l2  -0.440      0.153    -2.87   4.52e- 3  -0.741     -0.138
#> 5 rate     unemp.l2  0.673      0.148     4.55   9.03e- 6   0.382      0.964
#> 6 rate     rate.l2   0.123      0.0726    1.70   9.10e- 2  -0.0198     0.266
#> 7 rate     const     0.00517    0.238     0.0217 9.83e- 1  -0.465      0.475
glance(fit)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 8
#>       K     p  nobs logLik   AIC   BIC    HQ max_root
#>   <int> <int> <int>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1     3     2   213  -338.  731.  822.  768.    0.946
augment(fit)
#> # A tibble: 215 × 10
#>    date        infl unemp  rate .fitted_infl .resid_infl .fitted_unemp
#>    <date>     <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl>         <dbl>
#>  1 1953-01-01 1.69    2.9  1.96       NA         NA              NA   
#>  2 1953-04-01 1.45    2.7  2.19       NA         NA              NA   
#>  3 1953-07-01 1.01    2.6  2.04        1.51      -0.498           2.80
#>  4 1953-10-01 0.981   3.1  1.38        0.969      0.0114          2.76
#>  5 1954-01-01 1.33    4.9  1.18        1.02       0.309           3.46
#>  6 1954-04-01 1.30    5.9  0.97        1.17       0.131           5.61
#>  7 1954-07-01 0.909   5.8  0.72        1.06      -0.151           6.17
#>  8 1954-10-01 0.709   5.7  0.98        0.747     -0.0373          5.61
#>  9 1955-01-01 0.685   4.9  1.22        0.625      0.0593          5.49
#> 10 1955-04-01 1.06    4.7  1.59        0.898      0.165           4.47
#> # ℹ 205 more rows
#> # ℹ 3 more variables: .resid_unemp <dbl>, .fitted_rate <dbl>, .resid_rate <dbl>

fit$B is the (Kp+d)×K(Kp+d)\times K coefficient matrix (lags first, then constant; one column per equation), fit$Sigma the residual covariance (degrees-of-freedom corrected), resid(fit) the residuals, and lag_matrices() the K×K×pK\times K\times p array of lag matrices.

s <- summary(fit)
round(s$r.squared, 3)
#>  infl unemp  rate 
#> 0.983 0.949 0.928
round(lag_matrices(fit)[, , 1], 3)
#>         infl  unemp   rate
#> infl   1.538 -0.281 -0.057
#> unemp -0.010  1.330 -0.021
#> rate   0.546 -0.647  0.777

summary(fit) prints the full equation-by-equation tables. Standard errors are OLS standard errors with covariance Σ̂⊗(X′X)−1\hat\Sigma\otimes(X'X)^{-1}. For Wald and Granger tests and residual diagnostics (which start from augment(fit)), see Sections 4-5 of vignette("var-theory").

4. Stability

A VAR is stationary if all eigenvalues of the companion matrix lie inside the unit circle. stability() returns their moduli.

round(drop(stability(fit)), 3)
#> [1] 0.946 0.946 0.746 0.746 0.432 0.139

The largest modulus (0.95, also max_root in glance(fit)) is close to one: typical for macro levels, and a reminder that long-horizon results are sensitive to small changes in persistence.

5. Impulse responses with bands

irf() defaults to a recursive (Cholesky) identification in the column order of the data (infl, unemp, rate) and a residual bootstrap with 68% and 90% bands. The rate is ordered last, so it is the “monetary policy” shock that responds to inflation and unemployment on impact but does not affect them on impact. Other identification schemes (long-run, sign restrictions, proxies, heteroskedasticity) are in vignette("identification"), “Structural identification: from Cholesky to proxies and sign restrictions”. To choose a different order, use tidyselect: id_chol(order = c(rate, infl, unemp)).

ir <- irf(fit, horizon = 16, nboot = 500)      # bootstrap, Cholesky
ir
#> <varm IRF> K = 3, horizon 0..16, id = chol, bands: 68%/90%

The point estimate is in $estimate (response x shock x horizon, horizon 0 = impact), bands in $bands (response x shock x horizon x quantile), and tidy() gives the same information as a tibble with columns response, shock, horizon, estimate and, for each band, level, conf.low and conf.high. normalise_to() rescales a shock, for example to a one percentage point rise in the rate, and cumulative accumulates responses of variables entered in differences. Use ci = "wild" if residual volatility changes over time (it does here: the Great Moderation), "mc" for fast asymptotic bands, and ci = "none" for point estimates only.

ir1 <- irf(fit, horizon = 16, ci = "wild", nboot = 500,
           normalise = normalise_to(rate, rate, 1))
autoplot(ir1, shocks = rate) +
  labs(title = "Responses to a 1pp policy-rate shock") +
  theme_varm()

autoplot(ir) draws a response-by-shock grid as a ggplot2 object (rows: responding variable, columns: shock) and takes tidyselect shocks = and responses = arguments to subset. plot(ir) is a thin wrapper that prints the same plot.

autoplot(ir, shocks = rate)

The shaded areas are the 90% (light) and 68% (dark) pointwise bands: after a policy-rate shock, the rate decays slowly (own-persistence of about 0.9 per quarter), unemployment rises with a lag, and inflation moves little and with wide uncertainty.

6. Forecast error variance decomposition 

fv <- fevd(fit, horizon = 16, ci = "none")
round(fv$estimate[, , 17], 2)    # rows: variable, columns: shock, horizon 16
#>         shock
#> response infl unemp rate
#>    infl  0.82  0.16 0.02
#>    unemp 0.27  0.69 0.03
#>    rate  0.40  0.26 0.34

Each row sums to one. At horizon 16, about 80% of the forecast-error variance of inflation comes from its own shock, whereas the rate is explained roughly 40% by inflation shocks and 26% by unemployment shocks. Bands for FEVDs (fevd(fit) with a bootstrap) are wide, since they are ratios of squared IRFs.

7. Historical decomposition

hd() splits the observed path into a baseline (deterministic part and initial conditions) and the contributions of each structural shock. autoplot() stacks the contributions as columns and draws the actual series as a line; tidy() returns the long table (time, response, shock, contribution, actual).

h <- hd(fit)
dim(h$contributions)             # time x variable x shock
#> [1] 213   3   3
max(abs(h$actual - h$baseline - apply(h$contributions, c(1, 2), sum)))   # exact identity
#> [1] 4.440892e-16
autoplot(h, responses = unemp)

8. Forecasts

forecast() iterates the VAR forward. The default bands are predictive: they combine parameter draws (asymptotic Monte Carlo) with simulated future shocks.

fc <- forecast(fit, h = 12, nboot = 500)
round(fc$mean[c(1, 4, 8, 12), ], 2)
#>      infl unemp rate
#> [1,] 2.72  4.92 4.62
#> [2,] 2.66  5.23 4.25
#> [3,] 2.80  5.35 4.22
#> [4,] 2.99  5.39 4.34
autoplot(fc, n_history = 24)

9. A Bayesian VAR in three lines

bvarm() fits a conjugate Normal-inverse-Wishart VAR with a Minnesota prior (shrinking towards a random walk in levels). The result plugs into the same irf(), fevd(), hd() and forecast() generics, now with posterior bands. The MCMC sizes below are deliberately small to keep this document fast; use thousands of draws in practice.

b <- bvarm(y, p = 4, prior = prior_minnesota(), ndraw = 500, nburn = 200)
ib <- irf(b, horizon = 16)
round(ib$estimate[, "rate", c(1, 5, 9, 17)], 3)
#>         h
#> response     0      4      8     16
#>    infl  0.000 -0.033 -0.069 -0.102
#>    unemp 0.000  0.014  0.061  0.038
#>    rate  0.683  0.374  0.225  0.081
autoplot(ib, shocks = rate)

Hierarchical priors (prior_minnesota(hyper = "full")), stochastic volatility (bvarm(sv = TRUE)), triangular samplers (prior_triangular()) and are covered in vignette("bayesian-var"), “Bayesian VARs: priors, samplers and diagnostics”. Time-varying-parameter VARs (tvpvar()) are in vignette("tvp-var"), “Time-varying-parameter VARs with stochastic volatility”.

10. A local projection in three lines

lp() estimates the impulse response directly, with one regression per horizon and Newey-West standard errors, with no dynamic model to get wrong.

l <- lp(y, shock = rate, horizon = 16, lags = 2, contemp = c(infl, unemp))
round(l$estimate[c(1, 5, 9, 17), ], 3)     # horizon x response; a unit shock to the rate
#>      infl unemp   rate
#> 0   0.000 0.000  1.000
#> 4  -0.022 0.028  0.596
#> 8  -0.075 0.194  0.174
#> 16 -0.569 0.071 -0.435

l$estimate is a horizon-by-response matrix for a one-unit shock to rate, with l$bands and l$se alongside. With contemp equal to the variables ordered before the shock, this is the local-projection analogue of the Cholesky VAR response; compare it with irf(fit, normalise = normalise_to(rate, rate, 1)). autoplot(l) plots the projection and tidy(l) returns horizon, response, estimate, std.error and band columns.

autoplot(l)

See vignette("local-projections"), “Local projections and the LP versus VAR trade-off”, for instrumental-variable LPs, simultaneous (sup-t) bands and the comparison with VARs, and vignette("lp-advanced"), “Advanced local projections: state dependence, smoothing, panels, joint inference and forecasting”.

11. The tidy workflow

Everything above returns tibbles on request, so summaries and custom graphics need no special tools. Two examples. First, a coefficient plot from tidy(fit) with ggplot2, using the confidence limits that conf.int = TRUE adds:

co <- co[co$term != "const", ]
ggplot(co, aes(estimate, term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), colour = varm_palette(1)) +
  facet_wrap(vars(response), labeller = label_both) +
  labs(x = "Coefficient (95% confidence interval)", y = NULL) +
  theme_varm()

Second, tidy(irf) into a hand-built plot. The bands are stacked in rows, one per level; the point estimate repeats on each of them. Here we compare the wild bootstrap (ir1 above) with the asymptotic bands for the response of unemployment to the 1pp rate shock, and summarise the peak response:

ir_mc <- irf(fit, horizon = 16, ci = "mc", nboot = 500,
             normalise = normalise_to(rate, rate, 1))
both <- rbind(
  cbind(tidy(ir1), method = "wild bootstrap"),
  cbind(tidy(ir_mc), method = "mc")
)
u <- both[both$response == "unemp" & both$shock == "rate" & both$level == 0.9, ]
ggplot(u, aes(horizon, estimate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, fill = method), alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = varm_palette(2)) +
  labs(x = "Horizon (quarters)", y = "Unemployment response (pp)", fill = "90% band") +
  theme_varm()


# peak response and its horizon, from the same tibble
pk <- u[u$method == "wild bootstrap", ]
pk[which.max(pk$estimate), c("horizon", "estimate", "conf.low", "conf.high")]
#>    horizon  estimate     conf.low conf.high
#> 80       8 0.1025438 -0.004052864 0.2175228

The same pattern works for tidy(fc) (forecasts), tidy(h) (historical decomposition), tidy(l) (local projections) and tidy(b) (Bayesian posterior summaries); glance() gives one-row summaries (glance(fit), glance(b)). The outputs are plain tibbles, so base R (aggregate(), split()) and dplyr verbs work on them directly.
